title: DACA and TPS Holders Face Tougher Travel Rules After Immigration Appeals Board Ruling
excerpt: The August decision overturns a 12-year-old rule — advance parole trips can now trigger three- or 10-year bars on reentry to the United States.
body:
• In August, the Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that immigrants who have accumulated more than 180 days of unlawful presence may trigger three- or 10-year bars on reentry if they leave the United States — even when traveling with advance parole, according to WGBH.
  • The decision, Matter of Delcarmen-Lara (August 13, 2026), overturns the 2012 Matter of Arrabally and Yerrabelly rule that DACA and TPS holders had relied on for more than a decade.
  • The ruling is prospective only: it does not undo protection for people who already traveled on advance parole. Advance parole costs at least $575, with a possible new $1,000 fee upon reentry — and advocates urge anyone affected to consult an immigration attorney before booking travel.
  • USCIS defends the ruling, saying leaving the US can have immigration consequences for people with unlawful presence, and that advance parole never guaranteed readmission — the final call rests with CBP officers at the port of entry.

Immigrants in the United States who hold Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) or Temporary Protected Status (TPS) could face far greater difficulty traveling abroad under a recent immigration court ruling concerning "advance parole" — a reversal that practitioners say upends more than a decade of settled practice.

In August, the Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that immigrants who have accumulated more than 180 days of unlawful presence in the US may trigger a three- or 10-year bar on reentry if they leave the country, even when traveling with advance parole, according to reporting by WGBH picked up by immigration analysts.

What changed

For years, DACA and TPS recipients relied on the 2012 Matter of Arrabally and Yerrabelly precedent: an advance parole trip did not count as a "departure" that triggered the unlawful-presence bars. The August decision in Matter of Delcarmen-Lara overrules that protection. Now, for anyone with more than 180 days of unlawful presence on record, a routine family visit or medical trip abroad can activate a bar that keeps them out for years.

https://x.com/ARLnowDOTcom/status/2106399472557175116

The ruling has created acute uncertainty for immigrants waiting for green cards or seeking to adjust their immigration status. Many DACA and TPS recipients use advance parole to temporarily leave the country for family visits, medical treatment or other reasons — trips that were previously understood to be safe.

"The decision could leave thousands of immigrants unable to complete their green-card applications from within the United States. Some could potentially face a 10-year wait before being allowed to return."

— Robin Nice, immigration attorney, quoted by EthnicJournal

The government's defense

US Citizenship and Immigration Services defended the ruling, saying that leaving the United States can have immigration consequences for people who have accumulated unlawful presence. The agency also said that an advance parole document does not guarantee admission back into the country — the final decision is made by US Customs and Border Protection officers at the port of entry.

The ruling is prospective only, meaning it should not undo protection for people who already traveled on advance parole before the decision — a significant qualification for the hundreds of thousands who have made such trips over the years. About 538,000 people held active DACA status as of September 30, 2024, according to USCIS data; renewals continue for existing beneficiaries, though new applications remain blocked by litigation.

What it costs, and what to do

The filing fee for advance parole is at least $575, while some travelers may also face a new $1,000 fee upon reentry, according to EthnicJournal. Immigration advocates describe the change as creating an impossible choice for many DACA and TPS recipients: risk traveling abroad and potentially being unable to return, or remain in the United States and forgo seeing family members overseas.

Advocates are urging immigrants affected by the ruling to seek qualified legal advice before making international travel plans. That counsel matters now more than ever — the legal landscape that governed advance parole for 12 years no longer applies.

Diaspora angle

Indian immigrants are a smaller but real share of the affected population: thousands of Indians hold DACA or are navigating adjustment-of-status pipelines where an advance parole trip was once a standard, low-risk step. For Indian families split across continents — elderly parents in India, working children in the US — the ruling raises the stakes of every travel decision.

What's next

Litigation over the ruling is likely, and immigration attorneys expect challenges to its reasoning. In the meantime, the practical guidance is unchanged from the advocates' warning: do not travel on advance parole without an individualized legal assessment. A decade-old playbook no longer applies.
